results.abstractText: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) enables the three-dimensional visualization of molecular architectures within complex biological environments in a near-native state. In recent years, major advances in sample preparation, instrumentation, data acquisition, and computational processing have considerably expanded the scope of cryo-ET. Workflows that were once low-throughput and largely restricted to a small number of thin specimens and use cases can now be applied to many different samples from isolated macromolecular assemblies to cells, organoids, or tissues. In parallel, the advent of (i) automatic procedures for cryo-focused ion beam milling used for sample thinning as well as streamlined tilt series acquisition, (ii) improved methods for high-pressure-frozen specimens including lift-out, (iii) together with increasingly integrated reconstruction and processing pipelines are all contributing to improve throughput, reproducibility, and accessibility of the technique. Emerging deep learning tools further facilitate target identification, quality control with feedback loops, tomogram reconstruction, and downstream analysis by sub-tomogram averaging. Here, we discuss recent developments on different aspects of the cryo-ET workflow that are progressively bridging molecular and cellular scales in conjunction with multi-modal imaging. We also highlight current limitations and emerging technologies that may further extend cryo-ET capabilities, particularly in combination with complementary approaches toward integrative structural cell biology.

results.abstractText: High-resolution structure determination of RNA remains a major challenge due to its conformational flexibility, intrinsic heterogeneity, and susceptibility to degradation. Although RNA plays central roles in gene regulation, viral replication, and cellular homeostasis, RNA-only structures represent a small fraction of entries in the Protein Data Bank. Overcoming the limitations associated with RNA has therefore required the development of innovative engineering strategies to stabilize defined conformations and facilitate structural analysis. In this review, we describe RNA engineering approaches that enable structure determination of medium- to large-sized RNAs by X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM. These advances include the use of stable tetraloops to promote proper folding and crystal packing, scaffold-based strategies employing tRNA and 5S rRNA for recombinant RNA production and stabilization, and bacteriophage Φ29 prohead RNA as well as group I and group II intron scaffolds to facilitate cryo-EM structure determination. Together, these approaches repurpose natural RNA structural features and host processing mechanisms into practical tools for RNA stabilization, large-scale production, and structural characterization.

results.abstractText:
Motivation

Determining the three-dimensional (3D) structure of proteins is a cornerstone of structural biology, providing essential insights into their underlying biological mechanisms and functional roles. Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis allows researchers to investigate biomolecules at near-atomic resolutions, unraveling the structure of biomolecular complexes. However, reconstructing high-fidelity 3D volumes from extremely noisy projections, particularly under the interference of structural heterogeneity, remains a challenging task. Traditional Fourier-domain methods often suffer from frequency-dependent signal attenuation and uneven information distribution. While recent deep-learning-based frameworks attempt to predict high-frequency components directly in frequency space, they are highly susceptible to noise and often introduce artifacts. State-of-the-art (SOTA) real-space method circumvents Fourier-domain defects, yet remains constrained by the inherent spectral bias of multi-layer perceptrons, as fixed positional encoding fails to sufficiently capture intricate high-frequency details.

Results

We propose cryoTriplane, a real-space 3D homogeneous reconstruction network that utilizes a hybrid spatial representation to adaptively capture fine structural details. By combining fixed positional encoding for noise-robust structural initialization with structure-aware positional encoding for high-frequency refinement, our method achieves 3D reconstructions that are simultaneously globally consistent and locally fine-grained. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations across five simulated and four real-world datasets demonstrate that cryoTriplane significantly outperforms existing methods in resolving fine structural features. Furthermore, validation through downstream atomic modeling underscores cryoTriplane's ability to recover high-quality density maps. Specifically, our method achieves sequence coverage improvements of 4.6% and 5.5% on the EMPIAR-10005 and EMPIAR-10492 datasets over the SOTA approach, respectively.

Availability and implementation

Our code is available at https://github.com/chengyr1999/CryoTriplane. The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.

results.abstractText: The AAA-ATPase VCP/p97 unfolds ubiquitylated proteins in key signaling and cellular homeostasis pathways, yet the mechanisms by which Ufd1-Npl4 and FAF1 adapters handle ubiquitin chains to coordinate substrate loading and processing remain unclear. Our cryo-EM study of p97-Ufd1-Npl4 and FAF1 engaging a substrate reveal interactions that drive substrate processing. While Npl4 is capped by distal ubiquitins, and the initiator ubiquitin can be traced from the Npl4 groove to the ATPase channel at near-atomic resolution, we find that the Npl4 tower adaptively responds to the configurational changes in the ATPase motor's spiral staircase. A helix in FAF1 together with the Ufd1-UT3 domain engage proximal ubiquitins while providing the necessary structural plasticity to accommodate this motion and deliver ubiquitins to Npl4's groove. Our study reveals the intricate, dynamic interplay between p97, Ufd1-Npl4, and FAF1 in efficient processing of ubiquitylated substrates.

results.abstractText: Cellular cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) offers powerful tools to reveal molecular architecture inside cells, but dense cytoplasm often obscures fine molecular features, especially in narrow neuronal projections. Here, we introduce the Ghost Neuron technique, a preparation combining brief hypotonic treatment with controlled mechanical rupture immediately before freezing, facilitating high-contrast imaging of neuronal ultrastructure within its neurite topology. By removing the plasma membrane and reducing cytoplasmic density, the method allows high-resolution structural analysis while preserving the overall geometry of neurites. The method allows structural information to be mapped back onto neuronal architecture. The preparation also releases endogeneous macromolecular complexes onto EM grids, creating particle-rich regions suitable for high-resolution structural analysis. Using Ghost Neuron, we resolved axonal microtubules at 3.59 Å and 3.9 Å resolution, distinguishing expanded and compact lattice states, and mapped these states as interspersed patches along individual microtubules within axons. We also resolved axonal actin filaments and identified cofilin-decorated actin. These results establish Ghost Neuron as a discovery platform for linking molecular structure to neuronal organization.

results.abstractText: All cellular RNA polymerases (RNAPs) across Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya share a conserved catalytic core, yet bacterial and archaeal-eukaryotic RNAPs diverged after separation from the last universal common ancestor. This evolutionary split produced distinct subunit compositions and fundamentally different requirements for external factors during transcription initiation. Bacterial RNAP relies on a σ factor, whereas archaeal-eukaryotic RNAPs require a more extensive set of general transcription factors (GTFs) to bind promoter DNA, unwind the duplex, and position the template strand within the active site cleft. Notably, despite the close structural similarity between archaeal and eukaryotic RNAPs, the requirement for GTFs became further specialized after the emergence of Eukarya. This divergence raises the question of whether differences in intrinsic conformational flexibility and dynamics of these RNAPs contribute to distinct promoter-loading pathways. In this study, we addressed this question using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to examine archaeal RNAPs from Euryarchaeota and Crenarchaeota alongside yeast RNAP II. Archaeal RNAP displays a highly dynamic DNA binding clamp domain that samples a broad spectrum of open and closed states, whereas RNAP II predominantly adopts a closed clamp state. Both archaeal and eukaryotic RNAPs can be found in stalk-bound and stalk-less forms. Comparative structural analyses further reveal a unique conformational transition in crenarchaeal RNAP associated with clamp opening. Together, these findings define the intrinsic clamp-conformational landscapes across the archaeal-eukaryotic lineage and suggest that evolutionary tuning of clamp flexibility and dynamics contributes to distinct GTF-dependent promoter-loading mechanisms.
